previous_tier: documented (a LOW stone wall held by Webb's brigade on Jul 3); inferred (pre-existing: no OR report describes building it); open gap (builder, 2-3 ft height, Copse height, 80-yd right-angle length)
pdf_claim: A farm wall, built by local farmers before the battle, originally about 2-3 ft high, forms the 80-yd right-angle wall held by Webb's brigade at the Angle; the Copse of trees was under ten feet high in 1863; the wall is present at frame one; any added rail or earth reinforcement is unverified and must be flagged.
corrected_claim: The wall itself is documented and pre-existing as a farm wall (the NPS calls it 'a low stone wall that divided the Leister and Frey properties' and 'the farm boundary wall'); it stood at 6.30 a.m. on 2 Jul, when Webb put the 69th Pennsylvania behind it, and was held by the 69th and 71st Pennsylvania with Cushing's battery on 3 Jul. Two statements of the row are wrong or unsafe as printed. (1) Reinforcement is not 'unverified': Hancock's report says the 69th and 71st stood 'behind a low stone wall and a slight breastwork hastily constructed by them', Haskell (3 Jul) says the men had 'patched it with rails from the neighboring fences, and with earth', and the NPS study (Georg 1981, citing the Comte de Paris and a 20th Massachusetts account) says earth was thrown over or against the wall and rails stood on top. The additions are infantry work built after 6.30 a.m. on 2 Jul and before the assault on 3 Jul (no clock is given), the wall under them is never animated as construction. (2) The 80-yd length of the right-angle return is not stated by any source: Haskell has 'about twenty or thirty yards', Bachelder (1870, 1873) 'fifty yards', and the Philadelphia Brigade address of 1891 'some two hundred and sixty feet' (87 yd); nothing reads 80. Height: no source reads 2-3 ft: a Confederate officer wrote 'about three feet' at the Angle but 4.5-5 ft where the wall was unbroken; Haskell says the wall was badly pulled down in places and low enough to make men kneel. The Copse: a participant says the oaks 'rose but little above my horse's head' and the NPS study reasons 'not more than eight to ten feet high' (inferred); the Stone Sentinels page (blocked host) was not read. A gateway or opening in the wall to the left of the 69th Pennsylvania is documented (NPS, from a 69th Pennsylvania man's letter of 1886): the wall is not continuous.

sub_claims.claim: A low stone wall stood where Webb's brigade (69th and 71st Pennsylvania) and Cushing's battery were posted on Cemetery Ridge; the 69th Pennsylvania was already behind 'a fence a little in advance of the ridge' when the brigade was put in position at 6.30 a.m. on 2 Jul; Hays's division on the right held a stone wall just below the crest and Harrow's right 'was covered by a stone fence'.

previous_tier: documented (stone walls at East Cemetery Hill held by Harris's 2nd Brigade, and on each side of a lane held by the 25th Ohio); inferred (that these are the PDF's wall wrapping onto Brickyard Lane; that they are pre-existing farm walls); open gap (the lane's name)
pdf_claim: A low stone wall at the north end of (East) Cemetery Hill wraps onto Brickyard Lane, with walls along the lane; inferred to be farm walls; Harris's brigade held the wall and von Gilsa's brigade the lane; present at frame one.
corrected_claim: Documented: stone walls on East Cemetery Hill held by Harris's Second Brigade, First Division, XI Corps: late on 1 Jul Harris took 'a stone wall on the right, and nearly at right angles with the Baltimore road'; on 2 Jul the 75th Ohio and 17th Connecticut stood at a stone wall (Harris's first report puts it 'south of the hill', an unresolved tension); at 7 p.m. on 2 Jul the 17th Connecticut was ordered 'behind a stone wall on each side of a lane, below the battery opposite the cemetery entrance' and later changed front 'behind a wall running at right angles with the one we had just occupied'; after the repulse Harris held 'the stone wall in the rear of and parallel with' the first with his left on the Baltimore road, and before day on 3 Jul moved right along the wall to join the First Brigade. The name Brickyard Lane and the lane walls are documented only by the NPS (captions of 1863 photographs: a stone wall and stone-and-rider panels along the east side of Brickyard Lane, viewed from East Cemetery Hill; a second wall dividing Study Field 1 and Menchy Field 2 'partly dismantled and relocated for defense works'). Corrections to the 2026-11-04 row: R247 is Maj. A. G. Brady of the 17th CONNECTICUT, a regiment of Harris's own brigade (not the 25th Ohio of 'the other brigade'); so the lane walls are held by Harris's brigade, not by von Gilsa's. No report places von Gilsa's First Brigade on a lane: its 41st New York sat behind a 'square stone fence' at the cemetery to the right of the Baltimore road (P-03). That the lane of Brady's report is Brickyard Lane is an inference (no source names both). Pre-existing farm walls: the NPS says the walls of the area are farm walls (dry-laid, from field clearing, property boundaries) and that battle modifications existed; no source names the builder or date of these walls; the photograph reading shows rubble lines of irregular height.

sub_claims.claim: Harris's Second Brigade (75th Ohio, 17th Connecticut, 25th Ohio, 107th Ohio) held stone walls on East Cemetery Hill: late on 1 Jul a stone wall on the right of and nearly at right angles to the Baltimore road; on 2 Jul afternoon the 75th Ohio at a stone wall (his first report: 'south of the hill') with the 17th Connecticut on its left; after the evening attack a stone wall behind and parallel with the first, left on the Baltimore road; before day on 3 Jul the brigade moved right along the wall to join the First Brigade.

pdf_claim: A stone wall stood on the east side of the Baltimore Pike at Cemetery Hill, a landmark in the guide's description, present at frame one.
corrected_claim: Confirmed with additions. Three XI Corps reports put a stone fence on the east (right, going toward Gettysburg) side of the Baltimore pike beside the batteries of East Cemetery Hill: the 41st New York bivouacked behind 'a square stone fence ... to the right of the road leading from Baltimore to Gettysburg' at about 22:00 on 1 Jul and 'took position on the stone fence, with the front to Gettysburg' at 4 a.m. on 2 Jul; the 58th New York stood 'behind a stone fence to the left of Captain Wiedrich's battery', right of the road to Gettysburg, at 6 a.m. on 3 Jul; the 45th New York assembled at the cemetery 'behind the stone fence' on the evening of 1 Jul. The opposite (west) frontage of the Pike at the national cemetery site was walled too: the NPS Cultural Landscape Report says the site's structures were stone fences along the road frontages, vernacular dry-laid walls of field stones, mostly low (two to three feet) and some topped with rails, and that in July 1863 photographs the stone fences along the Pike had been reconfigured as breastworks, the wall along the north side of the Menchy field being extended into the Pike (probably by the 82nd Ohio) and a stone breastwork across the sidewalk. Pre-existing is inferred (field-clearing walls, no construction account); the battle modifications are separate infantry works in the window 1-2 Jul. The Gettysburg Daily guide the PDF cites (GD-Housch) is a blocked host.
